Andrea Swenson and Sarah Pearson concluded their tenures on the Piedmont School Board after nearly nine years of service. Pearson and Swenson received accolades and thanks from colleagues, friends and fans during their final school board meeting on November 10. Mayor Bob McBain made initial comments. “I can speak on behalf of the entire city council and the whole city staff in saying how much we have valued and benefitted from your roles on the school board, and more broadly speaking, your roles in the community for the last few years,” he said. McBain, whose 8-1/2 year tenure on the city council also ends in December, hinted at the need for a city proclamation honoring the two board members. Swenson and Pearson have been part of many initiatives by the school district since 2012, none bigger than the $66 million H1 bond. The fruits of that labor came into fruition in the form of the new three-story, state-of-theart STEAM high school classroom building, with a second building to be constructed next to it for the new Alan Harvey Theater. While COVID-19 prevented a ribbon cutting ceremony, the new school environment with unrivaled views and technology will be a pleasant reward for students when they are allowed to return to campus. In sharing her vision of the future, Pearson said, “My hope is that every student in our district finds joy and becomes an engaged learner. It inspires me to see our students become leaders for change who think critically for themselves and for the benefit of all.” The portion of the board meeting honoring the two civic servants was filled with admiration and respect, often overflowing into tears from callers and board members alike. articles.text: Editor: During this season of gratitude, we want to express our heartfelt thanks to everyone in the Piedmont community who has supported or who is planning to support the Giving Campaign this year. To date, we have raised $2.3 million [of a goal of $3 million] from more than 850 families for this year’s campaign to create stronger schools together. We need your support. The news this week about our county and most of the state falling back into the purple tier, and about our schools not reopening as planned, is sad and frustrating. The pandemic’s impact on our schools feels acutely painful. We are tired of distance learning. We all want our kids to have a better educational and social-emotional experience. Despite the challenges of the 2020-21 school year, we remain 100% committed to fundraising for our schools. Why give now? We are taking a long-term view; we deeply value having strong schools for our kids in our local community. When there is a widespread vaccination and kids [can] return to full-day school in person, we want our kids to be able to return to the robust, excellent educational experience we have always had in Piedmont. The dollars we are raising for the Giving Campaign are essential for the ‘21-22 school year. We understand that many people would like to have their voices heard and withholding Giving Campaign dollars, on the surface, may seem like a logical way to take a stand. However, lack of funding hurts Piedmont students more than anyone else. If we don’t raise our targeted funding, we will need to cut the school budget in June by increasing class sizes and cutting programs. The only way we can have strong schools for our kids to return to is by raising these dollars. It has always been, and still is, up to us. We know that fundraising can’t solve all of the macro health and safety challenges ahead of us, but if we do our part now, we can put our schools in a position to thrive once again when this pandemic is behind us. articles.text: Before entering the ministry, I spent nearly 20 years owning and operating a construction business in Boston, Massachusetts. Some of my contracts were for new construction but a fair amount of my business involved renovation. As a result, I have always seen demolition as part of the process of creating something better. For me, the dust, the piles of debris and the disruption of life don’t bother me because I know it can lead to a better future. As the pandemic rages on with yet another wave of destruction, there are also dangerous riptides of division tearing at the fabric of our country. Being so divided as we are, it seems almost impossible to imagine a future where we, as a society, actually live up to our name, The United States of America. But there is also the very real question of whether we have ever lived up to that name. The threat many feel of becoming a disenfranchised voter is nothing new. For instance, how could our ancestors ever describe our country as The United States of America while black and female citizens were denied a vote?

articles.text: Alameda County named Dr. Nicolas Moss as its permanent Public Health Director on November 17. He served in an interim role since July after Dr. Erica Pan was elevated to be California’s lead epidemiologist. Moss served as the Director of the HIV/STD section of the Alameda County Health Department for 7 years, from April 2013 to July 2020, until he took over as Interim Health Officer. Prior to that, he served as the Director of Clinical Prevention of the HIV Prevention Section at the San Francisco Department of Public Health for two years. Moss trained as an infectious disease medicine specialist and medical epidemiologist for the majority of his career, and is credited with overseeing the county’s response to the COVID- 19 emergency. “Dr. Moss brings extensive knowledge in communicable disease and nearly 10 years of experience in leadership roles,” said County Health Care Services Agency Director Colleen Chawla. “His appointment provides deep knowledge of, and ongoing continuity in, our response to the COVID-19 pandemic.” Moss received a degree from the University of California at Berkeley, and his medical degree from the University of California at Irvine. He trained in internal medicine, infectious diseases and public health at the University of Washington in Seattle. “My number one priority is Dr. Nicolas Moss to protect and improve health by achieving equity through partnership, fostering safe and healthy communities, and promoting fair and inclusive opportunities for all residents,” Moss said.
articles.title: Dr. Nicolas Moss named permanent County Public Health Director

articles.text: Dry spell forecast in Northern California for next few weeks While a bit of wet weather has moved in across Northern California, state officials are not yet declaring that the historically destructive 2020 wildfire season is over. Wildfire season often ends around November 30, but global warming has already changed fire trends in the state. As of yesterday, Tuesday, November 24, Cal Fire has not ordered any of its 21 units throughout California to activate winter preparations, traditionally a signal that the wildfire season for the year is done. Representatives from the National Weather Service and Cal Fire met this month and suggested that Northern California’s wildfire season appears to be in its closing stages, but nothing was officially announced. In fact, meteorologists are concerned that the next few weeks will be unseasonably dry. “Although temperatures have been slightly on the cool side of average for the past couple of weeks, along with some modest Northern California precipitation – it’s quite clear that fire season (locally mitigated though it may be) is not going out without a fight,” climate scientist Daniel Swain wrote in a report this week. Dry conditions are expected statewide through the first week of December, and there are concerns that strong winds in Southern California will significantly increase wildfire risks in the lower third of the state. The 2020 wildfire season will be remembered as one of the most devastating in history across California and the entire western United States. In Piedmont, skies turned a ghastly orange hue in September due to an outpouring of smoke from several fires blazing in the region. Five of the top 20 largest wildfires in state history occurred this year. The August Complex Fire, which burned in and around Mendocino National Forest, was the largest wildfire in California history and the state’s first “gigafire,” meaning a fire that burns over 1 million acres. The fire, sparked by lightning in August, was declared 100 percent contained by Cal Fire on November 12 after burning a total of 1,032,648 acres. Even when the 2020 wildfire season is declared over, the Piedmont Fire Department encourages all residents to stay vigilant and prepare for fire emergencies. Piedmonters can learn how to prevent wildfires by visiting the PFD webpage of the City’s website and www.ReadyForWildfire.org. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: The annual Toys for Tots campaign has begun, and Piedmont Fire Department has placed a donation box by the front doors of City Hall. Residents are encouraged to drop off new, unwrapped gifts for children in the bin during daytime hours seven days a week. Last year, the Marine Corps Reserve, which sponsors the nationwide campaign, had 109 donation sites in Alameda County and collected 25,000 toys to kids in the county. “With the help of Piedmont residents, we’re hoping that we can see that number go higher this year,” said Fire Chief Bret Black. Firefighters will empty the bin at the end of each day. If residents wish to bring a large number of donations, call the Fire Department at 420-3030 to arrange for a firefighter to be there. The Toys for Tots drive will also be accepting monetary donations for the first time. Checks may be left with the Fire Department, but made payable to Toys for Tots, 2144 Clement Avenue, Alameda, CA, 94501. Wildfire season continues as November comes to close Dry spell forecast in Northern California for next few weeks By Barry Eitel While a bit of wet weather has moved in across Northern California, state officials are not yet declaring that the historically destructive 2020 wildfire season is over. Wildfire season often ends around November 30, but global warming has already changed fire trends in the state. As of yesterday, Tuesday, November 24, Cal Fire has not ordered any of its 21 units throughout California to activate winter preparations, traditionally a signal that the wildfire season for the year is done. Representatives from the National Weather Service and Cal Fire met this month and suggested that Northern California’s wildfire season appears to be in its closing stages, but nothing was officially announced. In fact, meteorologists are concerned that the next few weeks will be unseasonably dry. “Although temperatures have been slightly on the cool side of average for the past couple of weeks, along with some modest Northern California precipitation – it’s quite clear that fire season (locally mitigated though it may be) is not going out without a fight,” climate scientist Daniel Swain wrote in a report this week. Dry conditions are expected statewide through the first week of December, and there are concerns that strong winds in Southern California will significantly increase wildfire risks in the lower third of the state. The 2020 wildfire season will be remembered as one of the most devastating in history across California and the entire western United States. In Piedmont, skies turned a ghastly orange hue in September due to an outpouring of smoke from several fires blazing in the region. Five of the top 20 largest wildfires in state history occurred this year. The August Complex Fire, which burned in and around Mendocino National Forest, was the largest wildfire in California history and the state’s first “gigafire,” meaning a fire that burns over 1 million acres. The fire, sparked by lightning in August, was declared 100 percent contained by Cal Fire on November 12 after burning a total of 1,032,648 acres. Even when the 2020 wildfire season is declared over, the Piedmont Fire Department encourages all residents to stay vigilant and prepare for fire emergencies. articles.text: As Piedmont and Clayton engage in a friendly competition called the Census Challenge, Piedmont is still leading the state in 2020 census response rates with 90 percent of residents. Of that pool, 84.5 percent of residents responded online. As of press time, Clayton’s self-response is 88.9 percent, and 80.2 percent did so online. The two cities, which are about 23 miles apart, have nearly identical demographics. Both cities are comparable in population; Clayton, with 4,006 households, is slightly larger than Piedmont with 3801 households. In a front-page story in the Clayton Pioneer, the city’s weekly publication, Mayor Julie Pierce expressed readiness for a little friendly competition. “We’re determined to post the highest response rate in the state for the 2020 decennial,” Pierce told the Pioneer. “Clayton residents have a proud history of civic engagement and participation. We’re going to show Piedmont, and the rest of the state, just how engaged we are.” Pierce added that the stakes are very high for California this time around. “We could lose a congressperson. It’s essential that everyone be counted,” she said. Clayton resident and Census Bureau media specialist Pamela Michael explained the importance of responding to this year’s census. “The apportionment of legislators is based on census data. Each state is allotted two senators regardless of population, but your congressperson as well as state legislators is determined by the number of people in your given geography. It’s critical that everyone is counted in order for everyone to be represented,” Michael said. Residents had until July 31 to voluntarily respond to the census. On August 11, census takers began knocking on doors of households that have not responded, and the deadline to complete the census ended on October 15 this year. “This competition is a great way to engage our communities in an effort that is important to both our cities,” said Piedmont Mayor Bob McBain. “We need to reach out to all our residents to ensure that they have the chance to participate in the census. If a little competition can step up the effort, then we will have some fun and support a very good goal.” Mayor Pierce has promised a gift basket of Clayton-produced honey and other offerings should the town not come in first by the August 11 deadline. Piedmont’s prize has not yet been determined. California’s self-response rate is 69.6 percent, more than the national average. Alameda County had one of the highest response rates by county in the state, with 75.8 percent responding to the census, and 67 percent of that pool doing so online. Self-response data is available for viewing by county, city, and state, at https://2020census.gov/ en/response-rates.html.

articles.text: We’ve all been there: there’s no milk in the fridge and you need to go grocery shopping. Even though the store is only half a mile away, you jump into the car to make the drive instead of walking. It’s faster, convenient, and doesn’t matter that much in the grand scheme of things, right? Although it might feel that way, driving is hugely impactful in emitting carbon emissions. Transportation is California’s largest source of carbon emissions – about 41 percent of the total – and has been the largest since at least 2000. This is due to California’s infamous car culture. In a state of 39.5 million people, Californians have over 27 million drivers’ licenses. From 2000 to 2016, vehicle miles traveled in the state increased by 11 percent, even as emissions have decreased. This is largely due to SB 32 and subsequent updates, which helped make vehicle fuel standards more rigorous. As California is the fifth-largest economy in the world, laws that are passed here typically influence manufacturing decisions. Despite vehicles consistently becoming more fuelefficient, Californians are driving more, meaning that the percentage of emissions stemming from transit remains stagnant. Beyond California, transportation is a large source of emissions nationwide. In 2016, the transportation sector passed energy production as the largest source of carbon emissions nationally. Almost 60 percent of transit emissions stem from light duty vehicles like SUV’s, pickup trucks, and cars. Another 23 percent come from trucking. There are about 275 million vehicles in the United States alone. Although car emissions are an urgent climate issue, it’s tough to change the behavior of that many individual drivers. For that reason, states and the federal government are finding cleaner alternatives to the energy grid – another large source of emissions in the U.S. While many states have been working on this for two decades, changing how millions of drivers get around is more of an uphill battle. Changing how we produce energy from a few hundred power plants is an easier legislative task than taking a few hundred million cars off the road. That’s not to say that transportation solutions don’t exist. Throughout the country and especially in California there has been a push towards electric vehicles, or EVs. In 2019, almost 700,000 EV’s were sold in California alone. This push is designed to take advantage of the energy grid, which is becoming “cleaner,” to help solve the transportation problem, which is still “dirty.” Many of these issues don’t have a clear solution. Transportation is one of the top three highest emitting activities in Piedmont, which is why the City is encouraging drivers to switch to electric vehicles and cut usage of gas-powered cars. Public transportation, walking, biking, or even carpooling all emit fewer GHG’s than driving a traditional car. Reexamining activities that we take for granted can help make a difference. When it comes to a shared problem like climate change, solutions stem from actions we can all take. If you would like to learn about other ways to reduce your carbon footprint, sign up for the Piedmont Climate Challenge at: www. piedmontclimatechallenge.org. articles.text: The Piedmont City Council approved updating the Pedestrian Bicycle Master Plan adopted in 2014. This update, called Piedmont Safer Streets (PSS), is intended to improve the conditions on our streets while including an additional focus on traffic safety. This plan will detail specific steps to make streets safer for the growing number of people who are walking and bicycling in town. To assist with the plan, a Pedestrian and Bicycle Advisory Committee (PBAC), which has met in October and November, will advise staff and consultants with the development of the Safer Streets plan. The City believes that public participation is essential not only to ensure that workable decisions are made, but also to show trust in the planning process. With the goal of keeping the planning going through this pandemic, there are three opportunities for the public to provide input on safety needs and concerns. • Digital Community Workshop A zoom workshop is scheduled for Wednesday, December 9 starting at 6 p.m. The workshop will review progress made since 2014 and will include a community discussion on future directions. • Online survey A brief survey has been created to hear Piedmonters’ opinions on key questions concerning walking, biking, and traffic safety. Everyone who responds will be eligible to win a gift card at Mulberry’s Market. • Pinnable Map page Residents can post location-specific comments about walking, biking, and traffic safety, or even post your cool ideas and suggestions for improving street conditions. It’s another opportunity to win a gift card. For more information, contact Associate Planner Gopika Nair at gnair@piedmont.ca.gov. or details and to learn more about the Safer Streets project, visit Piedmont Safer Streets project website (https://www.piedmontsaferstreets.org/).

articles.text: “Calvin, life could be a lot worse…” – Calvin’s mom “Ya, but it could be a lot better too…” – Calvin –Bill Watterson, “Calvin and Hobbes” If 2020 was a logic problem, it would be something like this: “You are going down the river at 2 mph and your canoe loses a wheel, how much pancake mix is needed to reshingle your roof?” That just about sums up the year so far. Not a lot of it makes any sense. It has been single-handedly the slowest yet fastest year I have ever experienced. Throughout this year we have had a lot of sadness thrust upon us, but even through the sadness, we have seen some happiness. Like most of the Earth’s population, I watched many of my plans put on hold or completely canceled. I was supposed to go on tour with my choir to Canada, and on a vacation to Hawaii with my family for the first time in three years. Since March, we have been barred from going to school, with no end in sight. I rehearse Finnish songs on Zoom (that’s real fun) with a bunch of other lonely kids. The most entertainment I had during the fall was checking air quality on my battered phone my mom refuses to replace because she lost her job and is being frugal. Things are much worse for people who lost a loved one to Covid-19, or to police brutality, or in one of the many wildfires we experienced this summer and fall. Everyone has lost a piece of themselves. And now we as a human race are forced to put our heads together to figure out how to save ourselves from all of the problems that have been put on our shoulders. No one can carry all this weight by themselves, so we all need to support one another; that is how we will accomplish more. It may seem like there is too much chaos and confusion for there to be any good, but that’s not so. On November 3, 159 million Americans voted— the highest turnout since 1908. It looks like people were so fed up with our current head of power they decided to take matters into their own hands. On Saturday November 7, after four nail-biting days of waiting, America – and a large part of the world – rejoiced as Joe Biden was elected to be the 46th president. This comes after four years of waking up and being scared to look at the news headlines. Now, multiple agencies have announced they are close to developing a vaccine against coronavirus, and possibly ready by the end of the year. Maybe that means in the spring we will go back to school. We are about to have a holiday where you get to stuff your face with an immense amount of tasty food. Christmas is right around the corner (and my birthday is also soon). I guess one thing you could be celebrating is that your favorite columnist, who has given you quality content all through this year, managed to get through 2020. Let’s talk gratitude. There are always things that people should be grateful for. Even if it’s just finding the airpods you lost in the beginning of the year. Or maybe being grateful for not getting sick with The Rona. I am grateful for going from a D- in French to a B+, and for getting a 90 on my test in math. I’m grateful for a chance to jump into a hotel pool in my clothes, because my parents allowed me I know that it’s not the New Year yet, so why am I doing a flashback? This is Thanksgiving, and we’re supposed to reflect back on the things that happened. Here’s one: 2020 feels like whoever the greater power is, he just fell asleep on the job, or maybe, he got bored, and instead of spreading these events over the next 10 years, just typed in: “Put everything in one year.”
articles.title: What are you thankful for?

The house at 801 Magnolia Avenue had several occupants after Frank Havens. On October 19, 1910, the Oakland Tribune advertised a two-bedroom, two-bath furnished bungalow for lease at the location. Ads in 1912 listed “woman wanted” for cooking, laundry and sewing. In 1920, the census recorded that a woman named Lenora K DePuali lived at 801 Magnolia Avenue with her teenaged son, married daughter, husband, nephew, and servant. Gail Lombardi, co-chair of the Piedmont Historical Society, said that the house must have grown in size during that time. The DePauli family members lived in the house from at least 1920 to 1926. The 1930 census showed six people living in the building: Granville and Florence Abbott, Eugene and Ruth Ebey, their daughter Florence Ebey, and a servant. The Abbotts moved there in 1933, and the Ebeys left in 1934. Architect Noble Newsom, of the Newsom Brothers firm, occupied the residence briefly, from 1935 to 1937. Despite his architectural profession, Newsom did not remodel the property. “Until the Piedmont Historical Society acquired the church history, I had always assumed that Newsom had remodeled the house. However, the attached photo is dated 1928 in the church history,” Lombardi confirmed. Photo of the building at 801 Magnoiia Avenue in 1928 when it was a residence. The First Church of Christ, Scientist recorded the building’s history from there. They purchased the building at 801 Magnolia Avenue in 1928 as a temporary building while they continued to search in the city for a permanent location. After several years, church members decided that the property would be satisfactory as a permanent church. They hired architects Morton Williams and Ralph Wastell to remodel the house. The church built a separate structure in the 1960s as a Sunday School. The city purchased the property from the church in 2003, but it was sparingly used because of structural and maintenance problems. In those years, it had fallen into disrepair. A small group of residents proposed to the city council in 2011 that under the name Piedmont Center for the Arts they would operate as a non-profit with the goal of creating a cultural arts center for the entire city. articles.text: Nikka Piterman, a former Piedmont resident and Piedmont High School graduate in 2012, was selected by the Republican Party as its candidate to challenge Barbara Lee for California’s 13th Congressional District in this year’s general election. The race ended with the likely winner, Lee, taking the seat; but the process of running a campaign was, for Piterman, an “overall positive experience.“ In order to get on the ballot in California, a candidate must meet a variety of state-specific filing requirements and deadlines. An individual can seek the nomination of a state-recognized political party, as an independent, or as a write-in-candidate. To gain the backing of the Republican party, Piterman met with local party leaders. “Typically you get a number of signatures from people in the party. It was about three or four months before we started collecting signatures [from the public] then I met with the local GOP, and they welcomed me with open arms and encouraged me to run,” he said. He added that he was surprised to find out that two years ago there were approximately 40 districts in California with no Republican representation. Democratic incumbents and candidates ran largely unopposed, or against write-in candidates. The process then began with gathering signatures. To run for California’s 13th Congressional District required obtaining 2,000 signatures by the filing deadline U.S. state. Piterman would like to see a referendum in Puerto Rico to ensure voluntary admission, and then upon admission, grant Puerto Rico with two senators and four representatives. He also sought to allocate five percent of the defense budget to the U.S. Space Force, and reclassify marijuana as a Schedule V substance. Piterman’s political aspirations began in high school in Piedmont. His involvement with the PHS debate club, the Junior Statesmen of America, was formative. In his final years of high school he served as Debate Club president and oversaw its growth from five members to nearly 40. Piterman confirms that he wasn’t expecting the race to come close, especially to political powerhouse Lee, now in her 12th congressional term. “I’m proud to say that we didn’t spend more than $10,000. pages.text: 8 Wednesday, November 25, 2020 By Allyson Aleksey The building located at 801 Magnolia Avenue has gone through several hands over the last century before coming under the ownership of the City of Piedmont. The Piedmont Historical Society has maintained a record of the various occupants from the 1870s to the current day. The first records of occupancy begin with real estate developer Jesse Wetmore. In 1878, he and his wife Matilda built a summer retreat in the Piedmont hills at 342 Bonita Avenue, at the corner of Bonita Avenue and Vista Avenue. The Historical Society noted that it had a wide veranda on three sides that caught summer breezes, a welcome relief from the dust and noise of downtown Oakland. Wetmore then built a slightly smaller summer home next door (now 801 Magnolia) for his daughter, Blanche Sherman. Blanche and her children traveled to Piedmont to spend the summers in the hills. She moved to the residence permanently after her husband died unexpectedly in 1881. In 1898, Blanche sold her cottage to Frank C. Havens. Havens purchased the property of the old Piedmont Springs Hotel, which had burned to the ground in November 1892. He planned to restore the grounds into a park and wanted to live close to the property to supervise the construction. Havens lived at 801 Magnolia History of Piedmont Center for the Arts 801 Magnolia Avenue over the last century Avenue from 1898 to 1909 while he built his own mansion at 101 Wildwood Gardens. The house at 801 Magnolia Avenue had several occupants after Frank Havens. On October 19, 1910, the Oakland Tribune advertised a two-bedroom, two-bath furnished bungalow for lease at the location. Ads in 1912 listed “woman wanted” for cooking, laundry and sewing. In 1920, the census recorded that a woman named Lenora K DePuali lived at 801 Magnolia Avenue with her teenaged son, married daughter, husband, nephew, and servant. Gail Lombardi, co-chair of the Piedmont Historical Society, said that the house must have grown in size during that time. The DePauli family members lived in the house from at least 1920 to 1926. The 1930 census showed six people living in the building: Granville and Florence Abbott, Eugene and Ruth Ebey, their daughter Florence Ebey, and a servant. The Abbotts moved there in 1933, and the Ebeys left in 1934. Architect Noble Newsom, of the Newsom Brothers firm, occupied the residence briefly, from 1935 to 1937. Despite his architectural profession, Newsom did not remodel the property. “Until the Piedmont Historical Society acquired the church history, I had always assumed that Newsom had remodeled the house. However, the attached photo is dated 1928 in the church history,” Lombardi confirmed. Photo of the building at 801 Magnoiia Avenue in 1928 when it was a residence. The First Church of Christ, Scientist recorded the building’s history from there. They purchased the building at 801 Magnolia Avenue in 1928 as a temporary building while they continued to search in the city for a permanent location. After several years, church members decided that the property would be satisfactory as a permanent church. They hired architects Morton Williams and Ralph Wastell to remodel the house. The church built a separate structure in the 1960s as a Sunday School. The city purchased the property from the church in 2003, but it was sparingly used because of structural and maintenance problems. In those years, it had fallen into disrepair. A small group of residents proposed to the city council in 2011 that under the name Piedmont Center for the Arts they would operate as a non-profit with the goal of creating a cultural arts center for the entire city. It was the first such endeavor since the early 1900s with some arts and music being offered in what is now Piedmont Park. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. articles.text: Cameron Smith (right), 27, was the first golfer to shot all four rounds under 70 at The Masters. He is pictured with his caddy, Matthew Tritton. Golf’s Masters Tournament knows no competition. Since 1934 it is the year’s most anticipated tournament, providing players and fans with four days of utter solace. Augusta National is the name of the course, possibly the most exclusive course in the world. Every hole looks like an edenistic garden. This year’s tournament was played to empty galleries from November 12-15. My grandfather once asked a friend if he could get onto the course. The golf pal from Georgia said maybe. Some years later his friend called back, “Hey I got you tickets to go watch The Masters Tournament.” My grandpop replied, “Huhn, I don’t want to watch the tournament, I want to play the course.” To wh ich h is f r ie nd replied, “What! Play it? That’s impossible!” As a members only country club, Augusta frequently has been in the spotlight for being overly exclusive. This year, the tournament directors stepped up their celebration of diversity. The first Black man to play on the course, Lee Elder, was honored throughout the tournament, in person and on the telecast. The tribute added a welcome touch to remind people that golf is played by young and old, man and women, and people of all identity. The tournament was easily won by Long Ball Dustin Johnson, who led the final day and set a course record with a score of -20 through the four days. After messing up a little to start Sunday, Johnson recovered and it really wasn’t close for the last four hours The lack of pressure at Augusta felt unnatural, unholy for the world’s biggest tournament. Usually the crowds go crazy and half the players totally cave to the pressure towards the end. But that was not the case due to a very limited capacity of fans which made it feel like a walk in the park. As it happens more times than not, the players I’m rooting against end up winning. I’m just grateful the tournament happened. Johnson, already ranked #1 in the world, probably would have slogged his caveman frame around oblivious to the happenings even if there was a crowd. The feel good stories which kept me watching came from two young golfers, Cameron Smith and Sung-jae Im who tied for second. Smith, an Australian, wears a scraggly imposter mustache that looks like it’s glued on, and his caddy looks more like a guy from a fishing boat that is slowly sinking into a swamp. Smith played valiantly, like a haggard wizard would, but Johnson had too great of a lead. Im, a 22-yearold from South Korea, had style and composure. He possibly has the coolest hat in all pro sports, it looks like a trucker hat from some made up company. Im’s perfect form and unflappability earned him just over $1 million for four days work. So The Masters happened, a storied event with more than a slice of history. The food and drink concessions remain at old school prices, and were just recently raised to $1.50 or $3.00 for a sandwich. Beer prices remain cheaper than at Whole Foods, all the more shame a large crowd couldn’t get rowdy in their khakis and visors. The Masters can be best understood by noting the expulsion of one of golf’s most colorful and popular TV commentators Gary McCord. While reporting at Augusta National the announcer with a curved mustache audaciously said, “There are some body bags down there, if that keeps going,” when a ball was rolling back off a green and toward Rae’s Creek. He also joked that “bikini wax” was being used to make Augusta National’s greens too slick for abal to stick. That resulted in McCord, then reporting for CBS, being banned from the course for life. That was in 1994. The ban has not been lifted. They’re serious at The Masters.

articles.text: Jimmy G’s future?; Raiders fall short; Premier League update; sad new for Warriors The Raiders nearly pulled off its second upset of the Kansas City Chiefs, but lost 35-31 after Patrick Mahomes led KC back with 1:44 remaining. Meanwhile, the 49ers come out of the bye week and look ahead to the Los Starting with the 49ers, you’d be hard-pressed to predict an SF upset over the Rams regardless if players come back from injury this week. Instead, we’ll examine the future of quarterback Jimmy 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan said last week that he “expects” Garoppolo to be the team’s starter in 2021. Meanwhile, Jimmy G has a no-trade clause in his contract until March 2022, so SF couldn’t deal him without his agreement. Reading between the lines, the 49ers are equally unlikely to find a team willing accept Garoppolo’s $25 million salary, find a partner which would trade them a first- or second-round pick, or have the quarterback waive his clause. Shanahan’s declaration of continuity makes sense from a Photo courtesy of NBC Sports What is the future of 49ers’ quarterback Jimmy Garoppolo? Cutting Garoppolo creates $24.1 million in cap space, but they’d receive a third-round 2021 compensatory pick at best if he signed with another team on the open market. Considering Garoppolo would be the top QB in the 2021 free-agent pool if released, SF wouldn’t move on from him unless they already had an option ready to roll for the season-opener. Given all those circumstances, the 2021 NFL Draft and Garoppolo restructuring his contract is the 49ers’ best bet. Flat out, if Shanahan sees an opportunity to improve at the position, he will take it. Currently projected at No. 12 in the next draft, SF could drop into the top- 10 and acquire a top-quarterback prospect while hoping Garoppolo gets his act together. If this season proved anything for Shanahan and the 49ers’ front office: the next-man-up is just as vital as the starter. Las Vegas Raiders The Raiders nearly proved us wrong a second time as we predicted the Chiefs to win another shootout on Sunday night. But now, the end of the season certainly favors Vegas with a matchup against the lowly Falcons in Week 12 and some easier games ahead. With Week 12’s game against Atlanta, stopping the passing attack is first and foremost. It has the potential to be another high scoring game if the Raiders’ defense doesn’t show up—but we’re going Vegas by over 14. Stanford: 123rd Big Game is this Friday Photo courtesy of California Golden Blogs The Golden Bears look to retain The Axe in Friday’s 123rd Big Game between California and Stanford. Here we are, the Wednesday before the 123rd Big Game between the California Golden Bears and Stanford Cardinal on Friday, November 27 at 1:30 p.m. Both teams limp into the game with 0-2 records and are looking mighty vulnerable. Of the two sides, the opening games have arguably left California the most devastated after getting bashed by UCLA 34-10 in Week 1 and upset last week by Oregon State, 31-27. The Bears held a 20-14 lead at halftime and were looking productive with 317 total yards at halftime. However, they could only amass 34 yards in the third and 88 in the fourth. Garbers struggled with accuracy you wouldn’t expect from a third-year starter, going 28 of 42 for 315 yards, three touchdowns, and two interceptions. Cal struggled mightily, showing that the lack of an offseason program has hit them harder than most programs. They had a pair of Nikko Remigio kick returns brought back due to penalties, each of which would have been touchdowns of 89 and 94 yards. Additionally, a blocked punt and a 24-yard shanked punt helped create Oregon State touchdowns. The Cardinal enter the Big Game with extra rest after its game with Washington State was canceled last week after a COVID outbreak within the Cougars meant they couldn’t field enough players. Cal has been rattled on defense after relying on a strong defense over the last few years under head coach Justin Wilcox. This could mean that Stanford will lean on quarterback Davis Mills, who went 31 of 56 for 327 yards and a touchdown against Colorado, though they lost 35-32. For NFL Draft enthusiasts, a notable matchup will be Bears cornerback Camryn Bynum squaring up with the Cardinal’s Simi Fehoko and other receivers. Given Garbers’ struggles to hit receivers, coupled with Cal’s COVID woes for its offensive line, it seems that Stanford could dial up a healthy dose of blitzes to keep the Golden Bears’ offense off balanced. For both programs at 0-2 and virtually out of the Pac-12 Conference championship and Bowl game appearances after its canceled games and losses, the Big Game becomes-essentially—each team’s biggest game of the season. “It certainly is different because of the unique nature of this season. But it doesn’t minimize the impact of the Big Game to our team, our fans - we know how much it means to us and everybody out there. We appreciate it for all that it is, regardless of these circumstances,” said Cal’s head coach, Wilcox. Photo courtesy of the Mercury News California struggled in its 31-27 loss to Oregon State. Meanwhile, the 49ers come out of the bye week and look ahead to the Los Angeles Rams. Starting with the 49ers, you’d be hard-pressed to predict an SF upset over the Rams regardless if players come back from injury this week. Instead, we’ll examine the future of quarterback Jimmy Garoppolo next season. 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan said last week that he “expects” Garoppolo to be the team’s starter in 2021. Meanwhile, Jimmy G has a no-trade clause in his contract until March 2022, so SF couldn’t deal him without his agreement. Reading between the lines, the 49ers are equally unlikely to find a team willing accept Garoppolo’s $25 million salary, find a partner which would trade them a first- or second-round pick, or have the quarterback waive his clause. Shanahan’s declaration of continuity makes sense from a business standpoint. Photo courtesy of NBC Sports What is the future of 49ers’ quarterback Jimmy Garoppolo? Cutting Garoppolo creates $24.1 million in cap space, but they’d receive a third-round 2021 compensatory pick at best if he signed with another team on the open market. Considering Garoppolo would be the top QB in the 2021 free-agent pool if released, SF wouldn’t move on from him unless they already had an option ready to roll for the season-opener. Given all those circumstances, the 2021 NFL Draft and Garoppolo restructuring his contract is the 49ers’ best bet. Flat out, if Shanahan sees an opportunity to improve at the position, he will take it. Stanford: 123rd Big Game is this Friday Photo courtesy of California Golden Blogs The Golden Bears look to retain The Axe in Friday’s 123rd Big Game between California and Stanford. By Jonathan Comeaux Here we are, the Wednesday before the 123rd Big Game between the California Golden Bears and Stanford Cardinal on Friday, November 27 at 1:30 p.m. Both teams limp into the game with 0-2 records and are looking mighty vulnerable. Of the two sides, the opening games have arguably left California the most devastated after getting bashed by UCLA 34-10 in Week 1 and upset last week by Oregon State, 31-27. The Bears held a 20-14 lead at halftime and were looking productive with 317 total yards at halftime. However, they could only amass 34 yards in the third and 88 in the fourth. Garbers struggled with accuracy you wouldn’t expect from a third-year starter, going 28 of 42 for 315 yards, three touchdowns, and two interceptions. Cal struggled mightily, showing that the lack of an offseason program has hit them harder than most programs. They had a pair of Nikko Remigio kick returns brought back due to penalties, each of which would have been touchdowns of 89 and 94 yards. Additionally, a blocked punt and a 24-yard shanked punt helped create Oregon State touchdowns. The Cardinal enter the Big Game with extra rest after its game with Washington State was canceled last week after a COVID outbreak within the Cougars meant they couldn’t field enough players. Cal has been rattled on defense after relying on a strong defense over the last few years under head coach Justin Wilcox. This could mean that Stanford will lean on quarterback Davis Mills, who went 31 of 56 for 327 yards and a touchdown against Colorado, though they lost 35-32. For NFL Draft enthusiasts, a notable matchup will be Bears cornerback Camryn Bynum squaring up with the Cardinal’s Simi Fehoko and other receivers. Given Garbers’ struggles to hit receivers, coupled with Cal’s COVID woes for its offensive line, it seems that Stanford could dial up a healthy dose of blitzes to keep the Golden Bears’ offense off balanced. For both programs at 0-2 and virtually out of the Pac-12 Conference championship and Bowl game appearances after its canceled games and losses, the Big Game becomes-essentially—each team’s biggest game of the season. “It certainly is different because of the unique nature of this season. Tamalpais has well over 100 miles of hiking trails; from the steep and strenuous, to the relaxed and nature focused. For this week’s outing we walked 1.5 miles on the Dawn Falls Trail to the Southern Marin Line Fire Roud until reaching the Barbara Springs Trail and back to the car, making an easy but stunning 3.5- mile hike. Its Dawn Falls Trail is a short and popular 1.4-mile walk with over 510 feet in elevation gain to its main attraction, Dawn Falls. Although the “Falls” is more of a trickle given its only active during or after a heavy rain, the walk shows you what makes Mt. Tam so magnificent. At times, you will pass through narrow corridors of redwood trees that look like something out of a fairytale with the steam of cold air during these cold months. Starting at the Dawn Falls Trailhead on Madrone Avenue in Larkspur, the trail along the inactive Larkspur Creek is a palette of vibrant fall colors from maple leaves; redwoods tower over in every direction, while lush green moss covers every tree, stone, and branch. It is worth mentioning that the Dawn Falls Trail is a mostly slim passage, less than three feet wide, meaning you will have to be patient when passing by hikers and runners on weekends. Our 10 a.m. walk up to the falls passed a staggering 49 people in the 1.5 miles, passing another 34 people on the remaining two miles back to the car. For those conscious of personal space, continue on the Southern Marin Line Fire Road; a dirt road which is wide enough for two lanes of cars. Otherwise, you can continue up the Hoo Koo E Koo Trail and Blithedale Ridge trails, which will more than double your elevation gain to provide a workout of near 1,200 feet until re-intersecting with the fire road. You’ll get glimpses of Mt. Tam’s eastern peak from the fire road, a location we last visited over the summer. The 0.5 mile walk down the Barbara Springs Trail back to the car is a very steep 500 foot descent back with tree roots shooting out in every direction, so be wary. You’ll likely have to use your hands at point if you don’t have hiking sticks. Moss is a mean feature of this trail. articles.text: The San Francisco Ballet company will present its wellloved The Nutcracker during the holidays, but online. The timeless fairy tale, with music by Tchaikovsky and choreography by Helgi Tomasson, will be available for viewing online from November 27 through December 31. The showing will be encompassed in an interactive, virtual experience for family and friends from the comfort of your home. Watch San Francisco Ballet’s spectacular Nutcracker, streamed in high definition, and then take a backstage tour of the opera house. You can send holiday snapshots to friends and family, enjoy historical highlights of the Nutcracker, and learn steps from the choreography. The ballet company advises that this event is best experienced on Chrome browser on a computer, laptop, or iPad. The Nutcracker is one of America’s most celebrated ballets. It begins on a foggy Christmas Eve in 1915, with Drosselmeyer putting the finishing touches on a magical nutcracker doll. It’s his gift for the Stahlbaum family, who have invited him to join their holiday festivities. Customers drop by his shop for last-minute Christmas gifts and Drosselmeyer shows them toys and clocks. Later, outside the Stahlbaum house, as people hurry home to their Christmas revelries, Drosselmeyer arrives with his beautifully wrapped present. You can view a progression of the acts at https://www. sfballet.org/discover/backstage/ story-of-nutcracker/. Tickets went on sale November 17 and can be purchased at https://donate2.app/kbqBT1.

articles.text: The Youth Art Exchange, a shared creative practice between professional artists and Bay Area youth, is hosting its 10th annual San Francisco Youth Arts Summit. The Summit, titled Arts is Essential, is a celebration of young artists and their vibrant contributions to the creative and cultural fabric of San Francisco and the greater Bay Area. articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse is presenting Brian Copeland’s The Jewelry Box, available to stream this Saturday, November 28 through December 25. The comedy is a prequel to Copeland’s hit solo show, Not a Genuine Black Man, and follows young protagonist Brian as he heads to the “mean streets” of Oakland to buy his mom a Christmas present. When he finds the perfect gift – a jewelry box in the White Front store – six-year-old Brian sets out to earn the required $11.97 by Christmas Eve. The play follows Brian’s adventures as he scours the “help wanted” ads, applies for jobs, and collects bottles, inching his way Brian Copeland in the San Francisco Playhouse production of The Jewelry Box, streaming November 28 to December 25. toward the perfect Christmas gift. Copeland debuted his first one-man play, Not a Genuine Black Man at the Marsh in San Francisco. The play explored his childhood experiences as a member of one of the only African American families living in a predominately white suburb of San Leandro, California. Not a Genuine Black Man went on to become the longest-running solo show in San Francisco theatrical history with over 800 performances. The show has been performed in over 30 cities, including a critically acclaimed run Off-Broadway. The play is currently in television series development. To stream The Jewelry Box, visit https://www.sfplayhouse. org/sf ph /2020-2021-season / the-jewelry-box/.

articles.text: California Revels will return to Oakland for its 35th season of one of the Bay Area’s premier holiday events. This year’s presentation is Unruly Magic: A Spirited Celebration of the Winter Solstice. Families, friends and holiday revelers are invited to watch wherever they may be, as this year’s production is entirely online, and can be viewed from December 12-20 at www.californiarevels.org. It will stream in High-Definition on Vimeo and YouTube, with live interactive components on Zoom Audiences of all ages can celebrate the Winter Solstice with traditional music, dance, ritual, and folk plays, including the mesmerizing “Antler Dance.” The production features top musicians, actors, and featured performers. This year’s show includes Shay Black and Windborne Singers. Directed by Jeri Reed, newly filmed pieces are blended with archival footage to create a dynamic and moving feast for the eyes, ears, and spirit. The story of Unruly Magic Approaching the longest night of the year, a young Reveler turns to a magical staff to help her find a way through somber and troubled times. The staff, imbued with ancient lore, takes her on an adventure that isn’t quite what she had in mind. Magic and mystery, spirits and song take the reins for this journey of the heart. The ancient traditions of bonfires, rituals, dances, and songs that have sustained generations through struggle and celebration are rekindled this Solstice, proving that tradition – and magic – live on. The event is part of the Cal Performances at Home project that brings the arts into your home. Ma has performed as a soloist with orchestras around the world. He has recorded more than 90 albums and received 18 Grammy Awards. In addition to recordings of the standard classical repertoire, he has recorded a wide variety of folk music such as American bluegrass music, traditional Chinese melodies, the tangos of Argentinian composer Astor Piazzolla, and Brazilian music. Ma will be joined by acclaimed British classic pianist Kathryn Stott, who performs as a concerto soloist, recitalist and chamber musician. Her specialties include the English and French classical repertoire, contemporary classical music, and the tango. Yo-Yo Ma and Kathryn Stott will perform a concert this Friday hosted by Cal Performances. Stott and Ma have joined forces for a diverse concert recorded in mid-November at Taiwan’s National Kaohsiung Center for the Arts Concert Hall. Their Songs of Comfort and Hope, the program that will be featured this Friday, combines a wide range of selections from the piano and cello repertoire, with traditional and new takes on favorites. The program will be available to stream on demand through December 12. A pre-concert conversation will take place before the event, at 6:30 p.m. The streaming premiere will begin at 7 p.m. Cal Performances Executive and Artistic Director Jeremy Geffen will introduce Ma and Stott and will join them in conversation. articles.text: A Scene from Jurassic Park: Fallen Kingdom. Movie review by Chris Honoré It’s been some 25 years since the first Jurassic Park was released, directed by Steven Spielberg and based on the Michael Crichton book. The central idea was that cretaceous creatures, most especially the high-rise dinosaurs with those signature reptilian eyes, could be reproduced using engineered DNA. It was a massive hit that combined all the ingredients of horror and action filmmaking for a breathtaking experience. As well, there is a through line from, say, a film like Jaws to the Jurassic series where a predator is loose and humans, no matter how resilient or well-defended, are ultimately helpless. A sense of overwhelming vulnerability represents the genius of these stories. After all, teeth-filled jaws come in all sizes and the image of a person’s torso dangling part way out of a raptor’s mouth will cause viewers to pay attention. Each of the movies that have followed, in the aggregate, have created what has been a durable franchise, while giving audiences a rush of adrenalin as computer generated raptors, scarily smart, manage to get free and overcome all best efforts to contain them. Jurassic World: Fallen Kingdom is the second in what will be a trilogy that began with Jurassic World. The setup is fairly straight forward: Isla Nublar was devastated when once again the dinos got loose. What made World riveting was that the island was now a popular amusement park, all revolving around the reptiles. Of course, the dinos, now free, devastate the park and the tourists, who run for their lives. Finally, the island is abandoned to the animals. What has occurred in Fallen Kingdom is that a once dormant volcano is on the cusp of erupting. Claire (Bryce Dallas Howard) and Owen (Chris Pratt) are recruited by a long ago benefactor, Benjamin Lockwood (James Cromwell), to rescue the remaining dinos and transport them to another island habitat absent tourists and rides. But, as is explained, the plan is born of avarice and orchestrated by a nefarious Lockwood assistant, unbeknownst to Lockwood. The hidden plan is to put the captured dinos on the market to the highest bidder. So, instead of a pristine island, Claire and Owen are sent to the Lockwood compound, a massive, 19th century manor house. Claire, Owen, and their two aids, Zia (Daniella Pineadad) and Franklin (Justice Smith), manage to sneak a boat ride along with the animals. The exit from the island entails scenes of the island exploding as the volcano erupts, as well as a harrowing trip to the Lockwood home, a darkly gothic warren of spaces with a basement filled with cages where the dinos, to be auctioned off, are being kept. Assume this: what can go wrong will go wrong at the manor. The location is no longer an island, but a dark, atmospheric, three story house with a first-floor entry replete with museum quality dioramas of dinos in their prehistoric habitats. The dilemma facing Claire, Owen, and sidekicks, is how to rescue the dinos. Things go from dicey to very bad. What has always been a strength of Jurassic franchise is that there have been tweens or teens woven into the plot. Kingdom is no exception. Lockwood, so it seems, has a granddaughter, Maisie (Isabella Sermon), a tween who is terrified through most of the third act. In fact, one of the best scenes that kids will definitely relate to is Maisie, hiding under her covers with an Indoraptor (a designer raptor) standing over her bed, a long claw tapping the tile floor. A chilling moment. When I screen any of the Jurassic films, I have to remind myself that the prized audience is made up of youngsters. They show up to be scared and the challenge is always how to go about creating that creepy, terrifying feeling in all its variations. Discussing this point in an email exchange with Piedmont alum and co-writer, Colin Trevorrow, the director of Jurassic World, he wrote: “We have a responsibility to appeal to everyone around the world. These movies don’t belong to America, they’re global, and they need to incorporate universal themes that can connect with a hugely diverse audience. It’s not just about age – it’s diversity of experience, of context.” “Many movies have the luxury of appealing to one group. We have to think about everybody,” he wrote. Much of what takes place is leading to the final film. As Trevorrow wrote, “We can’t get to where we’re going without this…. The dynamic between the characters has completely shifted by the end of this story. The equilibrium of the planet has been altered. Nothing will ever be the same for them, or the world they live in.” Colin Trevorrow, is a Piedmont High grad who graduated from the Tisch Film School at New York University. Jurassic World: Fallen Kingdom. Directed by J.A. Bayona. Written by Colin Trevorrow and Derek Connelly. Starring Chris Pratt, Bryce Dallas Howard and Rafe Spall. 2 hrs., 9 min. Rated PG-13. articles.text: A Scene from Yoshifumi Kondo’s Whisper of the Heart. Movie review by Chris Honoré Whisper of the Heart is the first and only film by director Yoshifumi Kondo, protégé of Hayao Miyazaki. The narrative is based on the manga story of the same name, written by Hiragi Aoi. It is an engaging and sensitive tale, meant to carry on the Studio Ghibli tradition. Sadly, however, Kondo died unexpectedly in 1998 and Miyazaki returned to the Studio from an all too brief retirement. The film’s protagonist is Shizuku (Brittany Snow), a self-conscious, often shy 14-yearold girl, as well as the characters that surround her, all created with an aura that is often dreamlike. Shizuku lives in the Tama New Town suburb of Tokyo. A voracious reader, always curious, she studies the check-out cards in three of her borrowed library books and discovers, to her surprise, that they each had been read by an unknown boy named Seiji (David Gallagher). “Who is he?” she wonders. “What is he like?” she asks herself. And so, with her imagination in a whirl, her curiosity peaked, she begins to search for him instead of studying for her final exams and preparing to graduate from her junior high school with her best friend Kuko (Ashley Tisdale). One day she follows a strange cat to an antique shop. It’s a wondrous place, she discovers, owned by an old man named Nishi, who turns out to be the grandfather of Seiji, the boy she’s been obsessively looking for. Of course, the two meet and become friends. Shizuki soon learns that Seiji nurtures a dream of becoming a world-class maker of violins; however, he explains, in order to fulfill his dream he must travel to Italy and serve an apprenticeship. Shizuki is inspired by Seiji’s commitment to his goal, and comes to realize that more than anything she wants to write stories. Amazing stories. And so, she too begins to research, sitting at a table, hunched over a sheet of paper, worrying whether she has the right stuff to tell a compelling story. Meanwhile, her parents worry that her grades might suffer as they watch their daughter devote herself relentlessly to her task. Whisper of the Heart, a coming-of-age whisper, sweetly and slowly told. It examines first crushes, unrequited love, and the search for one’s true talent. The story is also held together by a supportive and romantic connection between Shizuki and Seiji, unexpressed until it almost misses making an interesting ending. Whisper of the Heart. Directed by Yoshifumi Kondo. Animé from Studio Ghibli. With the voices of Brittany Snow, David Gallagher and Ashley Tisdale. 1 hr., 51 min. Rated G. articles.text: A Scene from Pixar’s Toy Story 3. Movie review by Chris Honoré For all of its CGI-animated talents, and they’re considerable, Pixar (22 Oscars, four Golden Globes and three Grammys), the creator of the Toy Story franchise, has never forgotten that at the center of every project is a touching, compelling story. Since 1995, the adventures of Woody (Tom Hanks) and his crew – Buzz Lightyear (Tim Allen), Potato Heads (Don Rickles, Estelle Harris), Hamm (John Ratzenberger), Jessie (Joan Cusack), Rex (Wallace Shawn) – have captured the imaginations of moviegoers, both young and old. Unexpectedly, Toy Story 3 delivers not only a sweet tale, one that is wonderfully imagined, but also one that is nicely distressing. Visually, it’s a treat, a smorgasbord of crisp colors and seamless animation. Put simply, it’s brilliant moviemaking. The core story is simple, inspired, and immediately familiar: Andy is going away to college and is cleaning out his room. He opens up his toy box and ponders what to do with Woody and company, all deeply embedded in his childhood memories. Through a series of mistakes, the gang ends up at a day care center run by Lots-o’-Huggin’ Bear, a seemingly nice old guy who soon proves to be something else. And so begins a great adventure that is both comical and thrilling, touching on issues of loyalty, friendship, courage and seat-of-your-pants close calls. What adults will understand is that Toy Story 3 is a comingof-age story. Andy has grown up and yet still feels connected to his toys. They are, in a word, “keepers.” He can’t simply put them out by the curb. Yet he knows that he has to leave them behind in the same way he must leave his childhood (and his mother) behind. Kids will understand intuitively that much loved toys are to be treasured, the equivalent of a favored blanket. A doll or bear or a Woody are there, through thick and thin, and all those moments that comprise a childhood. These are wonderful themes. Toy Story 3 turns out to be the sweetest and best-told story in the series thus far. Toy Story 3. Starring the voices of Tom Hanks, Tim Allen, Joan Cusack and Don Rickles. Pixar Animation Studios. articles.text: The Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir raised $119,000 in their first virtual fundraising concert, Discovering Our Voices, on Saturday, November 14. The event featured Choir performances from the advanced Ancora and Ensemble choirs, including a performance of “Autumn Time” presented by 36 Choir alumni from around the country. Funds raised during the event, aided by a silent auction, will support expanded financial assistance. The funds ensure that all children and youth who want to sing with the Choirs can participate. Discovering Our Voices was planned and executed by Development Consultant Lillian Archer of the Archer Group, and by the Choir’s Benefit Auxiliary Committee headed by Roshmi Mukherji. Technical production was supported by Galas at Home. Wine was donated to the event by Lin Jia Asian Kitchen. “Without the physical limitations of a venue or specific extended time for the event, the virtual format expanded access and allowed us to show up together as an inclusive community,” said new Executive Director Keri Butkevich. “Our team did amazing work and the performances went beyond Discovering our Voices to lifting our spirits, while we raised critical funding to ensure every child can connect and grow in the Choirs as part of our East Bay musical family.” Artistic Director Eric Tuan commented that the virtual event did have newly positive effects. Choir family Ann Kim, Kailamae, Koa, and Stuart. “Although we missed seeing each other in person, holding the event virtually meant we could welcome Choir friends both old and new scattered all around the world,” he said. “It was particularly moving to hear alums raising their voices together in “Autumn Time” alongside the beautiful virtual choir performances by Ancora and Ensemble. The love and passion for the Choir was palpable throughout the entire evening - from the amazing support shown in the Fund-A-Need, to the deeply impactful testimonials from our singers, to seeing all the Choir memories being shared in the chat. It was a once-in-a-lifetime event and a memory I will always treasure.” Viewers can enjoy the performance on the Choir’s Youtube channel at https:// w w w.yout ube.com /chan nel / UCZADkdlvhc4Mjie9hhTcm_g. Participating from the comfort of their home are Kiran Beattie, Aparna Rao, Joshua Beattie, Amba Beattie.

articles.text: We have just received fabulous news from our friend the brilliant guitarist in Barcelona, Jaume Torrent, with whom Debbie and I have performed many concerts. He recently was elected to the Academy of Arts in Catalonia. This is similar to being knighted in England or getting elected to the Legion of Honor in France. His letter announcing this distinction follows: Dear Joe and Debbie: I am writing to tell you that last week I was appointed Academician of the Royal Catalan Academy of Fine Arts of St. George. It is one of the greatest distinctions that can be given to an artist in Catalonia [Barcelona], and has so far been awarded to musicians such as Eduard Toldrà, Frederic Mompou, Xavier Montsalvatge and Carlos Guinovart. It’s such an honor for me and it makes me very happy. Yolanda is also very excited. I’ve never thought about having a recognition of this level, and I still find it hard to believe I’ve been given it. Guitarist Jaume Torrent of Barcelona, Spain, a frequent performer at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, has been given highest honors for his years of contribution to music and music education. Due to the pandemic, the act of public appointment will not be until April or May next year. I’ll have to give a speech, and I’ll also play something to exemplize the analysis of my work. I know you’ll share my joy. –Jaume
articles.title: Jaume Torrent named to Academy of Arts in Catalonia

articles.text: There was a big argument, and It did involve a turkey, But it wasn’t in Washington. However, some things never change. The combatants were Thomas Jefferson, John Adams, and Benjamin Franklin as they battled for how fledgling America would choose its national bird. Tempers f lared. Jefferson wanted the dove, Adams the eagle, and Franklin the turkey. Franklin‘s reasoning was the best, but he lost – and so did his turkey. Thanksgiving is tomorrow… But don’t get ahead of me. I want to give you a tasty recipe for fried fish. Like Ben Franklin, I believe my reasoning is very sound. You see, the first Thanksgiving did not star the turkey. It featured mostly fish and wild game – but not turkey. So here is an easy and tasty fried fish recipe: You need a flat fish like petrale sole fillets. Moisten them with a little milk or buttermilk. Put 2 tablespoons of packaged pancake mix in a plastic bag and shake the fish in it – just to dust the fish. Then fry the fish fillets to a golden brown. How easy is that? A big potato is a good side dish or you can be fancy and serve potatoes au gratin. White wine, of course. I like baked apples for dessert, and sometimes chilled poached pears in red wine sauce. Enjoy your Thanksgiving… but probably with the “traditional“ turkey. Bon appetite.
articles.title: Wherefor the turkey

articles.text: Part 11 in a series In the history of Piedmont, two saloons have quenched the thirst of residents and visitors. One saloon was in a respected hotel. The other was fraught with problems. The Piedmont Springs Hotel was built to serve visitors to the Piedmont hills and the mineral springs in Piedmont’s Bushy Dell Creek. Built in 1871 as a first class resort, the hotel had 20 rooms and a main dining room with a crystal chandelier and velvet drapes. The Grand Saloon (for gentlemen only) had a long mahogany bar, billiard table, spittoons and a pot-bellied stove in the corner. The Grand Saloon gained brief notoriety in 1891 when the wives of some of Piedmont’s more prominent businessmen petitioned the county to rescind the hotel’s liquor license. The women objected to their husbands stopping for a drink on their way home. The license was never rescinded, and the Piedmont Springs Hotel continued to serve liquor for another year before it burned to the ground in 1892. A Mon Chateau Piedmont’s other saloon was A Mon Chateau. As far back as the 1870s, today’s Grand Avenue was known as Pleasant Valley Road. It ran through a very pleasant valley – sunny, free of wind, rolling hills, scattered trees – that extended from Lake Merritt into the Piedmont hills. It was the route that many early Oakland residents took from downtown Oakland to picnic in the Piedmont hills. Today, that road is Grand Avenue until it crosses the city line near Rose Avenue. It continues as Pleasant Valley Road in Oakland until it crosses Broadway and becomes 51st Street. In 1892, Axel R. Gruggel built a restaurant at the southwest corner of today’s Grand and Linda Avenues and served refreshments to these travelers into the Piedmont countryside. He called it “A Mon Chateau” (My Castle) and advertised it as a family resort and French restaurant. Taking advantage of the mild weather, he built a beer garden on the Linda Avenue side of the restaurant. During its first years, A Mon Chateau was a quiet, slow-paced retreat, but that changed with the 1906 earthquake. With the influx of San Francisco refugees to the East Bay, the surrounding land began to fill with new houses and residents. From 1903 on, A Mon Chateau had a series of owners with a series of troubles. Gruggel sold the restaurant to George Atcheson in 1903. He ran A Mon Chateau for a few years but encountered problems with his employees stealing liquor. In 1907, three bachelors began operating the restaurant. Thomas P. Fenton, George P. Mahoney and John F. Jennings lived on the second floor of the building and advertised it as “A pleasant place in Pleasant Valley [to eat dinner]. Dinner prepared by Emil Lotz, former chef of Poodle Dog, San Francisco.” Dinners were $1.00. Patrons were advised to take the Oakland Avenue streetcar, get off at Sunnyside Avenue and take a short walk to Pleasant Valley. The bachelor owners also advertised A Mon Chateau as a saloon and sold wine, liquor and cigars besides serving dinners. Soon, neighbors began objecting to what was becoming a boisterous saloon. When the new City of Piedmont (1907) passed its liquor licensing regulations, A Mon Chateau’s application for a liquor license was denied. Nonetheless, the three owners continued to sell liquor at A Mon Chateau without a liquor license. The following year in March 1908, all three were arrested and their liquor confiscated. Three months later in June of 1908, A Mon Chateau opened under new management and continued to advertise itself as a “First Class Restaurant and Family Resort.” New owners Seeger & Thomas continued to operate it as a restaurant, but without a liquor license the number of diners dwindled. In 1911, Rudolph Kohn took over the business. He sought a new way to attract more patrons. He called the former restaurant “The Piedmont Casino” and opened two rooms upstairs for those who enjoyed playing poker and faro. However, gambling was also illegal. The casino was raided in 1912, and nine card-playing patrons were arrested and fined $55 each. The casino closed shortly thereafter. Chateau had become the Grand Avenue Grocery Company, and business thrived. It may not have been a good location for a saloon, but it was an excellent spot for a grocery. Residents in the rapidly growing residential neighborhood could walk to the market at the corner of Grand and Linda Avenues. Proprietors changed, and the grocery business grew. By 1922, the grocery had become the Del Monte Market, run by Jack Ruedy and William VanLoo, who lived upstairs with their wives. The market sold meats, vegetables and delicatessen items. Ruedy and VanLoo added a new storefront, a drug store (Raymond’s Drugs), and built a bakery in the former beer garden to offer freshly baked breads to their customers. In 1930, George W. Leisz and his son Jacob H. Leisz were running the grocery store. The grocery store thrived until 1937 when new supermarkets began pushing out neighborhood grocery stores. articles.text: David Perez was always that man you wanted to sit next to at an event because you knew he’d make it fun simply being in his company. He could make anyone feel comfortable, special, and appreciated. He had the unique ability to magically connect with people from all walks of life. But first and foremost, David was the most dedicated husband and father. His life’s journey ended all too soon as he fell victim to complications from the COVID-19 virus and passed away on October 14, 2020 surrounded by his family. He was 68. Born and raised in Oakland by parents Jesus and Connie Perez, Dave was constantly surrounded by family and his siblings Jessie, Becky, Josephine, and Rick. From the scrappy streets of West Oakland to the famed house on Spruce Street, Dave grew up to be a marvelous man with strong family roots, impressive streetcred, and above all, integrity. Seemingly larger than life, he lived every day to the fullest. He knew that the key to a fulfilling life was to make the people around him happy. articles.text: The Cancer League’s 47th annual Holly Ball event will be held on December 4 but without the traditional dinner event at the Claremont Country Club. Jenna Caldwell, this year’s Holly Ball Chair, was committed to continuing The Cancer League’s fundraising tradition, but safely. pages.text: Wednesday, November 25, 2020 25 Having a pandemic of home repair problems? By Jim Gardner 2020 has been a difficult year for most of us to absorb. The pandemic, financial issues, the election- there have been a lot of anxiety-producing issues recently. Interestingly, this has spilled over into the field of residential structural repair. Given that for most of us our homes are our biggest asset and our safe haven, these observations can be very disconcerting, especially since their significance is not readily apparent to the untrained eye. Original foundation drainage is either non-existent or not functional unless it has been upgraded. Seismic improvements may be marginal or not present. The most common cause of many of these problems is the lack of downspout drainage. Rainwater dumping up against your house can be a major contributor to settlement issues. In spite of all of these inadequacies, most of our homes are quite hardy, and their design and construction keep them standing except in extreme circumstances. When should I be concerned? A majority of settlement issues occur due to inadequate drainage. If you do nothing else, make sure your downspouts drain away from your home. If you don’t have a downspout drainage system, at least attach some flexible black pipe (see Ace Hardware) to direct the water away from your house until the drainage is permanently addressed. Hairline or small cracks in walls, ceilings, concrete slabs and stucco, if not abundant, are normal and not a big concern. But if they become larger or increase dramatically in size or number, particularly in a short time frame, that may be indicative of a more urgent problem. More obvious problems such as substantial water in crawlspaces and basements, retaining walls that are leaning significantly, or concrete that is clearly in poor condition (i.e. chunks are coming loose or look badly deteriorated) should be addressed. If there are significant cracks or movement with porches and stairs, they should be checked underneath to make sure their structures are intact. Now is the time to become an expert Given that we are all spending more time in our homes, this is the perfect opportunity for us to learn more about how they work. It is not rocket science. Most home improvement problems are fairly straightforward. Our website at jimgardnerconstruction. com has a lot of useful information and photos on these subjects. Many homeowners are terrified to go under their houses, but after crawling around under thousands of them, I have never been bit by a spider or found a wild animal or anything scary to report. Our basements and crawlspaces will reflect what you are observing in your living spaces above. If they are damp, with poor concrete or have structural problems, these are often fairly obvious. Take pictures and notes on what you see under your home, and inside as well. If you have cracks and settlement create a logbook with photos and measurements of their location for future reference. The majority of people I meet are vague about when their issues developed, and it is the observation of problems over time that are important, since most of them are slow developing. This is even more important with newer homeowners as they have no history in their homes. If you do your homework, detailing conditions over time, you will have a better sense of what your house is trying to tell you and when you may need to address it with a professional.
