articles.text: Piedmont High alum Renzo Downey (class of 2015), headed to the Sunshine State after college to become a news reporter covering state government for FloridaPolitics.com. In addition to the global pandemic and an economic downturn, Florida is rife with contention over the topic of civil rights vs. law and order. All of this occurring in a critical battleground state for the presidential election makes Downey’s job well worth the stifling humidity and sunburns. Downey attended Northwestern University and graduated from its acclaimed Medill School of Journalism. As his collegiate tenure culminated Downey took part in Northwestern’s journalism residency in Austin, Texas to cover that state’s 140-day legislative session. After that he looked for an opportunity to cover politics in a state capitol, particularly eyeing California, Texas, Florida and Washington, D.C. – Renzo Downey He landed in Florida’s capitol, Tallahassee, as a part of a small news team of about 10 reporters throughout the state. Even before COVID he worked from home using a second bedroom as his office. “Most folks are joining our lifestyle now. The Orlando Sentinel and Miami Herald got rid of their newsrooms, not because they wanted to, but because of the cost,” Downey explained. It seems that about every four years Florida finds its way into the national spotlight as a hotly sought-after swing state in the presidential election. This year proved to be no different. “In the last three weeks of the campaign, right after Trump recovered from COVID, he came down here six or seven times. Multiple times a week we were covering the presidential race coming directly to our backyard,” Downey explained. Florida Politics, his employer, Piedmont alum and Florida political reporter Renzo Downey, pictured at the Tallahassee airport covering a speech by current V.P. Mike Pence. has its reporters aim for balanced coverage. “On the editorial side I would say we are more on the left, but in terms of the day to day news stuff, we try to be down the center.” Downey covered a memorable Mike Pence visit to Tallahassee prior to the election. “It was at the airport here, in one of the private hangars on a back runway. He just pulled in on Air Force 2, and literally ran from the plane to the podium. It was a little weird. It was the same day that they announced his own chief of staff had COVID. And there he [Pence] was, running in the light rain from the plane to the podium.” This year Florida was not at the center of a recount vote controversy, and though the state voted predominately Republican, there have been no “stop the steal” protests. “Those folks that would have been protesting are happy how Florida turned out, the GOP seems to be pretty proud of the work they put in, especially in south Florida by making up ground in MiamiDade county.” Downey has a bit of a respite heading into the holidays, but the news will ramp up in January. “They are doing pre-session committee hearings early this year, in January. That’s going to be every week basically up until the session starts in earnest in March, and then it’s 60 days of a true legislative session.” Downey anticipates a fiercely contested legislative session this year as bills are being introduced. “There will be a law enforcement protection bill, a kind of an anti-violent protest bill. It will call for things like increased jail time for certain violent activities during a protest. It is all a part of that law and order message,” Downey predicted. session starts, Downey will be loaded with controversial storylines to unravel. “A shocking, attention grabbing thing in that bill, is if a local government defunds the police specifically – not an across the board slashing – then the state can withhold grants and funding to the local government. It’s a defund the defund-ers type of thing.” Also anticipated in Florida is a bill where if you are in a car and start getting mobbed, if you then hurt somebody with your vehicle trying to escape, there is some level of immunity. “That’s definitely going to be one flash point. In addition to the global pandemic and an economic downturn, Florida is rife with contention over the topic of civil rights vs. law and order. All of this occurring in a critical battleground state for the presidential election makes Downey’s job well worth the stifling humidity and sunburns. Downey attended Northwestern University and graduated from its acclaimed Medill School of Journalism. As his collegiate tenure culminated Downey took part in Northwestern’s journalism residency in Austin, Texas to cover that state’s 140-day legislative session. After that he looked for an opportunity to cover politics in a state capitol, particularly eyeing California, Texas, Florida and Washington, D.C. “It’s never boring covering politics in Florida. That’s exactly why I wanted to be here.” – Renzo Downey He landed in Florida’s capitol, Tallahassee, as a part of a small news team of about 10 reporters throughout the state. Even before COVID he worked from home using a second bedroom as his office. “Most folks are joining our lifestyle now. The Orlando Sentinel and Miami Herald got rid of their newsrooms, not because they wanted to, but because of the cost,” Downey explained. It seems that about every four years Florida finds its way into the national spotlight as a hotly sought-after swing state in the presidential election. This year proved to be no different. “In the last three weeks of the campaign, right after Trump recovered from COVID, he came down here six or seven times. Multiple times a week we were covering the presidential race coming directly to our backyard,” Downey explained. Florida Politics, his employer, Piedmont alum and Florida political reporter Renzo Downey, pictured at the Tallahassee airport covering a speech by current V.P. Mike Pence. has its reporters aim for balanced coverage. “On the editorial side I would say we are more on the left, but in terms of the day to day news stuff, we try to be down the center.” Downey covered a memorable Mike Pence visit to Tallahassee prior to the election. “It was at the airport here, in one of the private hangars on a back runway. He just pulled in on Air Force 2, and literally ran from the plane to the podium. It was a little weird. It was the same day that they announced his own chief of staff had COVID. Pictured are: Stephanie Cox, Krasuandra Hunter, Ryan Wilcox, Ernestine Epperson, and Candi Zamora. The other day I was chatting with Judy, one of the residents at The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Community. She was wearing a light blue mask with peaches on it. I said to her, “I don’t think I have ever seen that mask before. It’s very nice!” Her eyes lit up and she said, “It’s new. I now have six double-sided masks. That means I now have twelve different looks to select from!” Last week another resident, Faye, walked by. She was wearing a black mask with white polka dots, a white blouse with black polka dots, a black cardigan sweater and black slacks. Her black and white earrings matched her necklace and set off the outfit perfectly - pure class. I told her so. Her response was, “A fashionable lady knows how to color coordinate.” The U.S. Center for Disease Control (CDC) regularly updates its website with ways to help prevent COVID-19. While it has long been suggested that mask-wearing primarily protects the “other person,” in the CDC’s scientific brief updated on November 10, the agency cites studies that demonstrate that cloth mask materials can also reduce the wearers’ exposure to infectious droplets through filtration, including filtration of fine droplets. It’s common knowledge that nobody likes or really wants to wear a mask all the time, but the science is clear: Mask wearing helps save lives. Since it is likely we will be wearing masks for some time to come, why not look at some fashionable masks that show your personality? That is exactly what the staff at The Lake Merritt decided to do. As it turns out, it’s fun. As a pet lover, Stephanie was happy to find a line of masks that pay tribute to our furry friends. The fact that the paw print is made from rhinestones makes it all the better. Who doesn’t like a little bling? Krasaundra said, “Wearing a more fashionable mask made me feel good. After the residents started complimenting me, the idea became fun. It challenged me to up my game!” She has several different masks, but one of her favorites is the elegant black mask trimmed with pearls shown in the photo. Ryan likes his cat mask because he enjoys “just the right amount of zany on my face.” He likes things that are fun. We asked Ernestine why the sparkles? She wears masks that glitter and sparkle because they match her personality. Candi is wearing an “Alice in Wonderland” mask that she designed and made herself. She saw the need for masks early on and began making them for friends and family. Residents noticed her beautiful creations and have been asking Candi to make masks for them as well. Fashion has always had a way of taking our wardrobe essentials and turning them into statement pieces. It’s no surprise that the protective face coverings we’ve been advised to wear to curb the spread of the coronavirus have quickly been embraced and beautified by the fashion world. Since we’re going to wear one anyway, why not join with the residents and staff of The Lake Merritt and consider something with a bit of pizzazz? You’ll have fun doing it. articles.text: The following letter was sent to Piedmont City Council on November 8. Editor: In August of 2011, I had the pleasure of playing in a trio of French horns for the dedication of the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Piedmont was then poised to enjoy the cultural and educational benefits of an arts performance and exhibition space in the center of town, something rather unique to communities of our size. My expectations were fulfilled. I watched and listened to the PCA’s offerings over the following years and was not disappointed. As President of the Berkeley Symphony, I was proud to see a chamber music series, Berkeley Symphony and Friends, take root at the Center. As a horn player, I was delighted to participate in the organization and performances of the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra, which is based at the Center. I am now troubled to read the words of those would replace the Center with such things as a commercial health club, arguing that the PCA was merely an ‘’interim solution.” Since when have the arts been an ‘’interim solution’’? I cannot think of a better long-term investment than an arts center in the middle of our town. A look at the 2019 calendar of the PCA shows that the Center has remained true to its mission to promote artistic endeavors within Piedmont. On that calendar I see a wide range of events involving performing and visual arts, some presented by visiting artists and some by members of the Piedmont community, involving persons of all ages. I see, among others, the Piedmont Choirs, Piedmont Chamber Orchestra, PHS Drama, student recitals, and recitals by established chamber music groups. I see frequent art exhibits. I have been in discussion with the Piedmont Recreation Department about the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra becoming an offering of the Recreation Department. However, the Recreation Department likely does not have the expertise or time necessary to maintain the PCA’s unique blend of professional arts offerings together with space and time for local artistic talent and artistic instruction. In short, we have a unique institution in our midst that has enriched and will continue to enrich the cultural life of our community. articles.text: The following letter was sent to Piedmont City Council on November 5. Editor: The Piedmont Center for the Arts has been one of the best things to happen to Piedmont during my 43 years as a Piedmont resident. My wife and I have enjoyed dozens of world-class musical performances in this intimate and accessible venue, a jewel in the center of town within walking distance of one’s home. The many top-notch jazz and classical concerts at the PCA have enriched the community immeasurably. The Berkeley Symphony and Friends series and the annual Piedmont Chamber Music Festival are highlights. As a retired professional musician (principal French horn in both the Oakland and Berkeley symphonies), I participated in inaugural performances during the PCA’s opening. But more recently, I have been part of a local group responsible for launching and running the fledgling Piedmont Chamber Orchestra, whose performances in the Center have thrilled capacity houses. The existence of the Center itself made the very idea of the orchestra possible, and, without the Center as its rehearsal and performance venue, this superb (if I may say so myself) ensemble would struggle to survive. The orchestra has been a great ambassador for the community. The orchestra is comprised of both professional and advanced amateurs, many of them Piedmont residents, and our audiences have come from throughout the Bay Area. There is an amazing reservoir of musical talent in our community that the orchestra has been able to tap, thanks to the Piedmont Center for the Arts. With great appreciation. –Stuart Gronningen

articles.text: Editor: Councilmember Betsy Andersen is quoted in last week’s story on the PCA lease as saying “the city had many years in which to initiate its own programming in the space but didn’t”. Technically correct but wrong when taken out of context. The City acquired the 801 building in 2003 in a condition that prohibited the city from using it; principally, 801 was not ADA compliant. The City conducted several structural assessments of the facility and included 801 in the annual Capital Improvements program. However, by 2009, the $2M cost overrun of the Piedmont Hills Undergrounding district and tax revenue decline due to the recession prohibited the City from making the necessary upgrades to the building. Now that the City has $5M+ in the Facilities Maintenance Fund it would be appropriate for the City to upgrade both wings of the building, making 801 a more usable and profitable space. –Garrett Keating

articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department received a report of a fall victim on Moraga Avenue on Thursday morning, November 19 at 8:24 a.m. Resident Patsie Kao was walking her dog on Moraga Avenue when two German Shepherds escaped from a yard and tried to attack her dog, a corgi. Kao fell to the ground in the act of protecting her dog. During the melee she suffered a dog bite puncture wound to her hand. Two witnesses responded to the scene quickly, upon hearing cries for help, and called the police and then the paramedics. Kao was treated by the paramedics and was taken to a hospital for emergency treatment for the bite wound. The corgi remains in high spirits, thanks to the quick action of Kao. The owner of the two dogs was notified of the incident, and the dogs have been placed on a 10-day quarantine at the house. The report of the incident has been forwarded to Animal Control Services.
